title: Safe inheritance in Java
idea: Inheritance done right means a subclass truly is-a kind of its parent, and the parent is designed for extension or marked `final`.
points: Use `extends` only for a real is-a that keeps every parent promise.
A subclass depends on parent internals, such as which methods call which.
Design for extension: `final` public methods plus documented `protected` hooks.
Otherwise mark the class `final` and offer composition instead.

messages.label: receiveAll(3 messages)
messages.note: The override counts the whole batch first, then delegates to the parent.

messages.label: super.receiveAll(batch)
messages.note: The parent loops and calls `receive` on `this` for each message.

messages.label: this.receive("hi")
messages.note: `this` is an `AuditedInbox`, so the subclass override runs and counts again.

messages.label: super.receive("hi")
messages.note: Only now is the message stored. It was counted twice on the way.

messages.label: this.receive(...) x2 more
messages.note: The same detour repeats for each remaining message in the batch.

messages.label: audited() too high
messages.note: The subclass broke because of a parent detail nobody documented: the self-call.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: A subclass overrides two methods and silently double counts because the parent calls itself.

walk.text: `Inbox` is neither `final` nor documented for extension. Anyone may subclass it.
`receiveAll` loops over `receive`. This self-call is an invisible detail.
The subclass counts each single message, a reasonable override on its own.
It also counts batches, unaware that the parent re-enters `receive`.
Compare stored and audited: the counts disagree, with no error raised.
If the parent later stops self-calling, the subclass breaks the other way.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: The parent fixes its flow with `final` methods and exposes one documented hook.

walk.text: The parent is abstract and keeps its list private. Subclasses cannot touch it.
`receive` is `final`: it validates, stores, then calls the hook exactly once.
`receiveAll` is `final` too, so its self-call is now a safe, fixed fact.
The hook is the only extension point, and its contract is written down.
The subclass overrides only the hook, and is itself `final`.
Batch and single calls now agree: each stored message is audited once.

pitfalls: Extending a class only to reuse code; if it is not is-a, compose instead.
Calling an overridable method from a constructor; the subclass sees its fields still unset.
Leaving a public class non-final without documenting self-calls; future parent edits break subclasses.

quiz.q: `Base` calls an overridable method from its constructor. What prints?
quiz.why: The `Base` constructor runs before the `Child` constructor body. The override runs on a half-built object, so `name` is still `null`.

takeaway: Extend only for true is-a, and only classes designed for it.
